Human consciousness sublates [aufhebt] in such a way that it keeps [aufbewahrt] and preserves [erhält], and therefore survives [überlebt] its being sublated [Aufgehobenwerden].

In its synthetic aspect, then, the human being unites the other two aspects: thesis and antithesis. Through memory, in the broad sense, a person remains connected to what has been given to them—to both the natural and the human or sociopolitical world. In this respect they remain connected to the thesis. But they are also free from this given reality insofar as they negate it in the antithesis.

The thesis becomes genuinely human only in the synthesis, because it becomes human only by passing through self-negation. The antithesis, by contrast, does not exist at all outside the synthesis, because the synthesis is the realization of the antithesis. An action becomes real in what it produces, and what it produces then becomes part of what already exists—that is, part of the thesis. So an action that has entered into reality in this way is itself a synthesis.

A revolution is revolutionary only because it negates the “old regime.” But it becomes real only by creating a “new regime.” And this new regime is synthetic or historical only because it contains both the “old regime,” in an essentially transformed form, and the revolutionary negation of that regime—which is itself essentially transformed in the process of becoming real.

Once a synthesis is complete and established, however, it has already become a thesis. It is not a thesis while it is still being created, and certainly not for the people who are creating it. It becomes a thesis only for those who encounter it as something “given”: something they did not “make,” something that was already fully formed before they arrived. It can then serve as the starting point for a new dialectical triad.
Still, we should repeat that a real human being is always synthetic, whether we happen to describe them as a “thesis” or as an “antithesis.”

As long as we are dealing with a human being, what is “given” to them always includes the memory of their historical past. And that historical past necessarily presupposes the negation of something that had once been given. At the same time, insofar as a human being exists, they are always something given as well. If they negated absolutely everything that was given, they would simply annihilate themselves.

Human existence is therefore always “dialectically sublated.” Most of its content consists of “memories” of the past: a past that has been abolished through negation, yet preserved within that negation, and in this way raised—once it has become conscious and free—to a “higher level.”

In other words, human existence is always “mediated.” Between a human being and what is given to them, whether natural or historical, there always stands the real or merely possible negation of that given reality. So even the decision to preserve what is given is, from one point of view, always “free,” because it presupposes choosing not to exercise a possible negation. To that extent, the given is “freely accepted,” and the person becomes “responsible” for it.

So when we say that a human being—or a society, or humanity as a whole—exists at some particular moment as a thesis, we mean only that what is given predominates. In particular, the “animal” side predominates. The person accepts this given reality more or less “unfreely” or “unconsciously,” because they do not even “see” the possibility of negating it.

A human being exists as an antithesis, by contrast, when the negation of what is given predominates—that is, when freedom or free action predominates. Such a person lives and maintains themselves within the existing world only in order to “overcome” it.

Finally, a human being exists as a synthesis when “totality” or “historicity” predominates: when they freely and consciously accept a given reality which, as they know and remember, was itself created through the negation of an earlier given reality.
But if this is true—if the human being is never anything other than a synthesis—then we can say that a human being is nothing other than free action.

For dialectic, and therefore synthesis, exists only insofar as “negativity” exists. And this negativity becomes real only in free, negating, and therefore creative action. The reality of dialectic is therefore the reality of action, in the strongest sense of that word.

But the reality of action presupposes three things. First, there must be something given toward which the action is directed: a given reality, or thesis, that is going to be changed—that is, partially negated. Second, there is the action itself, the antithesis. Third, there is the result of the action, the synthesis.
And this three-part structure of action is nothing other than the human being insofar as the human being is dialectical—that is, genuinely human, free, and historical.

To the extent that a human being has not “made” themselves—in the sense that they did not make their own body—they are an animal. And if their “action” consisted in a pure and complete self-negation, that is, suicide, they would be nothing.

So insofar as a human being exists as a human being, they have created themselves. This should be understood in the same sense in which Christianity could say, for example, that God created the human being “from nothing.”

A human being’s being is nothing other than their human existence, and that existence coincides with human action: action that is negative or free, and conscious. There can therefore be no difference between what a human being is and what they do.
Once we see this, it becomes clear that human existence is historical and therefore essentially temporal.

Action takes time. For action to occur, something must have already been, and something else must not yet be. There must therefore be a past and a future. Action itself happens in the “present”—that is, in time—precisely because the present contains, in some way, and presupposes both past and future.
So if a human being is nothing other than “realized action,” we can also say that the human being is “realized time.”

But why can we not say the same thing about natural “things”? Do they not also endure? Do they not also have a future connected with a past, as well as a present? Why should time not be essential to them too?

We can say that time is not essential to natural things because, although they exist in time, time does not exist in them—or, which amounts to the same thing, it does not exist for them, in their consciousness.
In particular, the future—the aspect that belongs most essentially to time and distinguishes time from space—does not exist for them.

Strictly speaking, only the present exists. There is therefore neither past nor future in the full sense. Neither is presently real. What “was” has already ceased to exist, while what “will be” has not yet entered existence.

Still, in a certain sense, the past is more real than the future. The past continues to form part of the reality of the present. It is fixed and unchangeable, and therefore “identical,” just as the present is.
The future, by contrast, is not real in this strong sense. What was, after all, really did exist. But what will be has not yet entered existence at all. It does not yet actually exist.

That is why we cannot say that the future is fixed or unchangeable. It cannot be definitively “determined.” In principle, it could be anything. And if the present is going to change, it is only because something new enters it from the future.
The future is therefore what produces change: it negates the present.
It, and it alone, is the “negative.”

In other words, if “negativity” can become real only in time—because to realize negativity is precisely to change what is given—then the time in which negativity exists is, above all, the future. The future is the negative moment or aspect of time.
And conversely, any time in which the future rules must itself be “negative,” or dialectical—that is, human and historical.

The future always “negates” the present by turning it into the past. But if the present or the past predominates, then whatever “new” thing comes from the future to replace the “old” present will itself be determined by what already exists. In other words, it will not differ from the old in any essential way. It is as though the present withstands the pressure of the future and remains what it already is and was.
Anything that “endures” in such a time will therefore remain “identical,” eternally equal to itself.

But if time is dominated by the future—by what does not yet exist—then the future negates the “old” present and replaces it with something genuinely new, something that was not already contained in the present. What endures in such a time therefore changes in an essential way; it becomes “negative.”

We can therefore say that non-dialectical, natural existence realizes a time dominated by the present or the past, while a time dominated by the future is realized only in dialectical, human, historical existence.

A time determined by the present or the past is therefore not dialectical. Its three basic moments or aspects—past, present, and future—do not form the dialectical triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. In a certain sense, they remain “identical,” because the future introduces nothing essentially new into the present, and the present therefore passes into the past without essential change.
This kind of time is realized only in natural, spatial-and-material existence, and the natural world exists only in this kind of time.

Take “inorganic” nature. It is obviously determined entirely by its present. If we know the present completely, then in principle we know both its entire past and its entire future, because both merely unfold what was already contained in some way in the present.

With “organic” nature, by contrast, knowing the present alone does not seem sufficient. But even if the present does not dominate biological time, neither does the future play an essential role. Biological time seems instead to be governed by the past.

Suppose we want fully to understand a chicken’s egg. We have to know that in the future it will produce a chicken and not some other kind of bird. But to know this we do not need to know the future. It is both sufficient and necessary to know the egg’s past: to know that it was laid by a chicken and not by some other animal.
More generally, if anything essentially distinguishes organic nature from inorganic nature, it is precisely this element of heredity: the predominance of the past.

A time dominated by the future, by contrast, is realized only in the non-natural world—that is, in the human or historical world. And historical existence, insofar as it is historical or properly human, exists only in this kind of time.
History is nothing other than real time in which the future predominates. And conversely, such time does not exist outside human history.

To understand more clearly what this predominance—or “primacy”—of the future means, and more generally to uncover the inner structure of human, historical, dialectical time, let us consider a concrete example and ask why a particular event occurring in the present is called “historical” in the ordinary sense of the word.
In other words: when and why can a particular “present” count as a “historical event” rather than simply as the current state of some thing at a particular moment?
Let us take the traditional example of the Rubicon.

Julius Caesar and his troops approach this Italian river. Caesar intends to march on Rome and seize power. Crossing the river will therefore mean revolution, civil war, and the transition to a new “regime”—the “imperial” regime.
On the night before the campaign begins, Caesar walks along the banks of the river. He considers the situation and makes his final decision: early tomorrow morning, his troops will cross the Rubicon.
In a certain sense, we can say that the Roman Empire was born that night. The night is therefore, at any rate, “historical” in the ordinary sense of the word.
Let us first look at what is happening in the “present”—say, at exactly midnight that night. What actually exists “for the moment,” at the same time as the river and its banks?
All we see is a particular individual walking beside the water.

And there is obviously nothing “historical” about that in itself. Any soldier in Caesar’s army could have been doing the same thing, for all we know. Caesar himself might simply have been walking because he could not sleep. If that had been the case, we would know nothing about it, and there would be nothing historical about it at all.
So if Caesar’s nighttime walk is historical, it is only because, while walking, he made the decision to march on Rome the next day.
That means he was thinking about the future: about something that did not yet exist.

It also means that this future was, in a certain way, “present” in his consciousness, and therefore in his “brain”—and only in his. It accompanied him, so to speak, as he walked along the banks of the Rubicon.
Although it remained future—that is, although it remained something that did not yet exist—it nonetheless had a real presence within the present, within what already actually existed.
And we should notice something else: this future was “revolutionary.” It “negated” the present because it was going to change it essentially.
There would have been nothing historical in Caesar imagining some future that followed naturally and necessarily from the existing present.
We can therefore say that it is the real presence of this kind of future within the present that makes the present “historical”—or, if you prefer, human.
And this means that in historical time, the future dominates, prevails, or rules.
But the mere presence of the future is not enough to make the present historical.
After all, anyone can walk beside a river at night dreaming of taking Rome and seizing absolute power: an ambitious young man, a dreamer, a “poet,” a utopian—or even a lunatic.

The presence of the future in such a present is certainly still “human,” because an animal cannot “dream” about the future. But there is nothing “historical” in a future of this kind if it is conditioned only by the present.
The Rubicon is historical only because the march on Rome was conceived by Caesar: by an individual who had a genuine “chance of success.”
And that also means bringing the past into the present.

Caesar’s “chances” are determined by what he had actually accomplished up to that point—by what he had done in the past. It is only because of his past that he is “Caesar” rather than a “dreamer” or a “madman.”

His thought is not a “dream,” and his decision is not a “whim,” only because he himself knows that past and takes it into account—along with everything it implies: his army, the balance of forces, and so on—when thinking about the future and making his decision.
So the past too, although it no longer exists, accompanies him as he walks beside the river. It too is present within the present, within what exists “for the moment.”
The present is therefore historical—genuinely real and, in the strongest sense, human—only when it includes both the future that negates it and the past that conditions it.
In other words, the historical present is “synthetic,” and therefore dialectical.

It is the result of a union, or synthesis, between the thesis on the one hand—that is, its “identity” with the eternally fixed past, or with the determinate character it has received from that past—and the antithesis on the other hand: the future that negates it.
It is now easy to see that in dialectical or historical time, the order of the fundamental “moments” is not the same as it is in natural time.
The historical present is not the source of the past and the future. It does not determine them. It is itself determined.
And it is determined not only by the past, but also—and above all—by the future.
The historical present is therefore synthetic or total: it is “dialectically sublated” and “mediated” by future and past.

It is also easy to see that this dialectical time is nothing other than the time in which human action takes place: action in the strong sense of the word, action that revolutionarily negates what is given and builds or creates a new reality.
An action is human—that is, “free” and “conscious,” rather than involuntary, instinctive, or merely reflexive—only insofar as it is “premeditated”: undertaken in order to realize a certain “project.”
It is creative only when this project is new—that is, when it refers to something that does not yet exist “in nature.”

And for that very reason it is “negative.” By introducing something new into what already exists, it changes what exists. It destroys the existing reality insofar as that reality is what it presently is and was.
Yet an action can actually exist, and a project can become real, only if the project is not “utopian”—that is, only if it takes account of what is and what has been.

So real action—successful action—always enters the present from the future, from a “project” that initially exists only in thought, while at the same time resting on the past: on previously acquired knowledge and experience preserved in memory.

That is why to say that a human being is nothing other than their free and creative action is also to say that the human being is the realization of a form of time in which the future enters the present through the past.
And conversely, such time becomes real and exists only in the form of human action.
So once again we see that dialectic is not a “method”: not a way of looking at reality, understanding it, and talking about it.
Dialectic is itself a particular kind of reality—namely, the human being and human history, and even the time in which that history unfolds.
